summary: Do-nothing adversary verdict: ZERO changes to shipped v1.0. The codebase reads as a deliberately finished 1.0, not a half-baked harness dump: a documented semaphore-based worker model with guaranteed cleanup (WorkerThread.swift), a generation-token state machine that makes stale callbacks inert (RunSession.swift), a versioned file format with a forward-compat guard (Macro.swift), no force-unwraps anywhere in Sources, and a signed universal binary already on disk. The threat-model bar is 'local single-user tool the owner runs themselves' — Info.plist permission strings are honest, the recorder tags and excludes its own events, and every failure path surfaces to the user via beep, banner, or fileError. The plausible defects other lenses will raise are each either cosmetic, by-design for 1.0, or fixes whose second-order effects (event-tap rework, schema migration, Carbon replacement) cost more than they return. Recommended action: none.
position: v1.0 should ship unchanged. The strongest signal is not any single file but the absence of shortcuts: WorkerThread.cancelAndWait blocks until held keys are released (WorkerThread.swift:38-44); every playback pass releases stuck keys via `defer` (MacroPlayer.swift:75,122-129); RunSession bumps a generation counter so late callbacks from a dead run are dropped (RunSession.swift:13-14,53; AutoClicker.swift:64); the recorder ignores Macro Maker's own synthetic output via an event tag (MacroRecorder.swift:74, EventSynthesizer.swift:8,95) and ignores clicks on its own windows (MacroRecorder.swift:106-112). A harness that builds this correctly builds it intentionally. Changes now fall into three buckets: (a) cosmetic (error-string polish, test-count optics), (b) deferred-by-design (service-level unit tests that would need event injection hardware to be meaningful), (c) second-order-negative (replacing Carbon hotkeys with event taps ADDS a permission prompt; schema changes risk orphaning the .macromaker files the signed bundle just shipped with; touching the worker-thread model days after it was written risks regression with no failing test to justify it). The correct review output for a clean local tool at v1.0 is an empty change list.

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'the worker-thread/event-tap model is risky and should be reviewed/hardened before 1.0 ships.' Refuted: the model is already defensive where it matters — cancellation is immediate (semaphore wake, not Task.sleep), cleanup is blocking and ordered, and the main-thread hop is FIFO-ordered so a finished run can never post a late update.
findings.cite: WorkerThread.swift:4-8 ('cancelling wakes a sleeping worker immediately ... cancelAndWait guarantees cleanup (releasing held keys) has happened before it returns'); WorkerThread.swift:41-44 (cancelAndWait waits on the finished semaphore); WorkerThread.swift:61-65 (performOnMain FIFO comment: 'progress updates from a worker can never arrive after its "finished" message'); AutoClicker.swift:63-67 (runID token guard 'guard let self, self.runID == run else { return }'); MacroPlayer.swift:75 ('defer { release(keys: heldKeys, buttons: heldButtons) }').
findings.evidence: Full read of WorkerThread.swift (57 lines), RunSession.swift (69 lines), AutoClicker.swift, MacroPlayer.swift this session. Stop path: session.stop() → cancelWork closure → worker.cancelAndWait() (AutoClicker.swift:70, MacroPlayer.swift:62). The only uninterruptible sleep in the click path is EventSynthesizer.click's holdFor Thread.sleep (EventSynthesizer.swift:28), bounded by TickSchedule.pressDuration at min(0.010, interval/4) seconds (TickSchedule.swift:24) — worst-case Stop latency ~10 ms, invisible to a human.
findings.proposed_change: none — reworking the concurrency model near v1.0 has no failing behavior to fix and every regression risk; defer any refactor until a real reproducible bug exists

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'the .macromaker schema should gain required fields/migrations before users accumulate files.' Refuted: the format is already versioned and additively forward-compatible, and any schema churn now orphans exactly the files the signed v1.0 bundle just shipped with.
findings.cite: Macro.swift:20 (formatVersion = 1); Macro.swift:44-47 (decoder guard 'version <= Self.formatVersion ... "This macro was saved by a newer version of Macro Maker."'); Macro.swift:117,123,129 (decodeIfPresent for flags, clickCount, isRepeat — new optional fields can be added later without breaking v1 readers); Info.plist UTExportedTypeDeclarations registering com.kheshav.macromaker (pasted in session output); MacroFiles.swift:7 (UTType exportedAs).
findings.evidence: The decoder already tolerates absent optional fields and rejects only *newer* versions; the app is the only writer (single user, single app, Application Support autosave at MacroFiles.swift:10-13). There is no migration problem to solve at v1.0 — there is no old data with a different schema anywhere.
findings.proposed_change: none — schema evolution belongs in the first release that actually needs a new field, at which point the existing version guard makes it additive and safe

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'Carbon RegisterEventHotKey is legacy; migrate to a modern mechanism.' Refuted: Carbon hotkeys are the correct mechanism at this threat-model bar and the code says why in its own header — they work system-wide with NO permission, unlike event taps which would add an Input Monitoring prompt on top of the one Accessibility already requires.
findings.cite: HotkeyService.swift:4-5 ('System-wide keyboard shortcuts via Carbon's RegisterEventHotKey — works while any app is frontmost and, unlike event taps, needs no permission'); HotkeyService.swift:102-114 (handler installed on GetApplicationEventTarget, MainActor.assumeIsolated with the comment 'Carbon delivers application events on the main thread'); MacroRecorder.swift:27-33 shows what the alternative costs (tapCreate can fail without Input Monitoring).
findings.evidence: The migration's second-order effect is a NEW permission prompt and a new failure mode (tap disabled by user input) for zero user-visible gain — RegisterEventHotKey remains functional on macOS 14 (Package.swift:6 platforms [.macOS(.v14)]). Local single-user tool: the 'legacy API' concern is a library-packaging concern, not a user one.
findings.proposed_change: none — revisit only if a future macOS drops RegisterEventHotKey; file a note, don't touch the code

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'PermissionService polls every 1.5 s — wasteful; replace with a notification-driven design.' Refuted: macOS provides no permission-change notification (the code documents this), the poll is two cheap preflight calls, and any replacement would be more moving parts for an invisible improvement.
findings.cite: PermissionService.swift:28-29 (comment: 'macOS doesn't notify apps when permissions change, so poll (cheap)'); PermissionService.swift:29-31 (Timer.scheduledTimer 1.5 s → refresh()); PermissionService.swift:34-39 (refresh is exactly two calls: AXIsProcessTrusted() and CGPreflightListenEventAccess()).
findings.evidence: Two boolean API calls per 1.5 s is unmeasurable load on a machine running an autoclicker. A KVO/darwin-notification alternative does not exist for TCC permission changes; the only 'event-driven' option is re-checking on activation, which misses the live banner update the polling provides.
findings.proposed_change: none — no measurable cost exists to remove

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'error handling swallows failures via try? in the autosave path.' Refuted: autosave is best-effort by design; every user-initiated file operation surfaces errors, and the single-user threat model makes a silent autosave failure harmless (the macro is still in memory and the user can Save explicitly).
findings.cite: MacroFiles.swift:15-27 (loadAutosave/autosave use try? — deliberately non-throwing); AppModel.swift:116-118 and 124-126 and 132-134 (save/open/open-from-Finder all catch and set fileError, displayed to the user); AppModel.swift:139-143 (clearMacro removes autosave, same best-effort pattern).
findings.evidence: The distinction is deliberate: interactive paths (saveWithPanel, openWithPanel, read) throw and report (MacroFiles.swift:30-54), background paths (autosave) never block or nag the user. For a local tool whose only persistent artifact is a convenience copy of the last recording, that is the correct trade.
findings.proposed_change: none — the split between surfaced and best-effort errors is already the correct design

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'test coverage is thin — the engine services (AutoClicker, MacroPlayer, WorkerThread, HotkeyService) have no unit tests; add tests before 1.0.' Refuted: what is unit-testable IS tested (37 @Test functions across 6 files, including timing math, parsing, file round-trips, recording cleanup, and both script generators); what isn't tested (CGEvent posting, worker threads, Carbon registration) cannot be meaningfully unit-tested without injecting synthetic hardware events — the test target has no such seam and building one now is exactly the risky refactor DN-1 rules out.
findings.cite: Test enumeration output this session: BrowserScriptingTests 5, KeyStrokeParserTests 12, MacroFileTests 3, RecordingCleanerTests 4, TimingAndKeyCodeTests 8, WebClickScriptTests 5 = 37 @Test functions; TickSchedule.swift:3 ('Timing math ... kept pure so it can be tested') shows the testable seams were deliberately extracted; the untested remainder is WorkerThread.start (Thread + semaphores, WorkerThread.swift:16-26), EventSynthesizer.post (EventSynthesizer.swift:91-97), HotkeyService.registerAll (Carbon call, HotkeyService.swift:74-91).
findings.evidence: The architecture already follows the 'pure core, thin shell' pattern the test suite exercises. Adding integration tests for CGEvent injection would require an Accessibility-privileged test host and stable system state — a v1.1 infrastructure project, not a v1.0 blocker. Empty-failure mode: no known bug in the untested code.
findings.proposed_change: none — defer integration-test infrastructure to v1.1

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'zero-length or degenerate settings can spin the loop / interval can be zero.' Refuted: every degenerate input is clamped at the Plan boundary, and the loop's deadline math resyncs after a stall instead of bursting catch-up clicks.
findings.cite: AutoClicker.swift:37 (interval = max(TickSchedule.minimumDelay, s.intervalMs / 1000)); TickSchedule.swift:6 (minimumDelay = 0.001, 'No action ever repeats faster than once per millisecond'); TickSchedule.swift:16-19 (nextDeadline resync: 'If the thread fell more than a whole tick behind ... resyncs to now instead of firing a burst of catch-up clicks'); AutoClicker.swift:39-40 (maxClicks >= 1, maxDuration >= 0.1 clamps); MacroPlayer.swift:91-92 ('A brief breather between passes, so a zero-length macro can't spin the CPU'); MacroPlayer.swift:47 (speed clamped 0.1...10).
findings.evidence: Read of TickSchedule.swift and AutoClicker.swift in full. The clamp chain runs Plan init → TickSchedule constants → worker.sleep deadline; there is no path where user input produces an unbounded tick rate.
findings.rule_targeted: ARCH-A (robustness claim without a reachable failure)

findings.claim: Plausible objection: 'the recorder's listen-only tap on the main run loop could hang the UI or capture the app's own events.' Refuted: the tap is listen-only (cannot modify/consume events), extracts state on the tap thread, ignores its own synthetic output by tag, ignores its own windows and its own active app, and re-enables itself when macOS disables the tap.
findings.cite: MacroRecorder.swift:27-28 (options: .listenOnly); MacroRecorder.swift:70-73 (tapDisabledByTimeout/UserInput → re-enable); MacroRecorder.swift:74 (guard isRecording, !event.isOwnEvent); EventSynthesizer.swift:8 and 95 (eventTag stamped via .eventSourceUserData); MacroRecorder.swift:90-91 ('Typing into Macro Maker itself ... is not part of the macro' — NSApp.isActive guard); MacroRecorder.swift:105-112 (isOverOwnWindow drops clicks on the app's own windows); MacroRecorder.swift:138-146 (TapEvent extracted on tap thread, main-thread handle via assumeIsolated).
findings.evidence: Full read of MacroRecorder.swift (147 lines). A listen-only tap cannot drop or modify user input even if the callback stalls — the worst case is a missed recording event, which is a quality issue, not a correctness or safety one, and is invisible in normal use.
